B000490.text: This week, the White House Office of Budget and Management’s Director, Russell Vought, appeared before the U.S. House Appropriations Subcommittee on Financial Services and General Government. During the hearing, I asked the Director about how Congress can be any clearer to ensure that the Trump Administration understands that once a funding bill is signed into law, the President is not allowed to change or second-guess the spending and withhold it due to policy or political differences. That is at the heart of Article 1 of the U.S. Constitution and why Congress also passed the Impoundment Control Act of 1974, when President Nixon tried to withhold funds that were already obligated according to the law.

This week, I asked the White House Office of Budget and Management’s Director, Russell Vought, to explain how poorly planned cuts to the federal workforce last year have weakened services and protections upon which Americans rely. This includes the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, which is responsible for protecting America’s agriculture from invasive species and diseases. USDA-APHIS began mounting a vigorous response to the resurgence of New World Screwworm – a deadly parasite affecting livestock – in 2024. However, in early 2025, the Administration illegally fired workers and forced others to resign, causing over 25 percent of all USDA-APHIS employees to leave. USDA’s New World Screwworm prevention, monitoring, surveillance, and control efforts were halted. USDA had approved $378 million in prevention and control funding for sterile fly facilities in 2023 and 2024, yet the money went unspent when the new administration paused funding. This is extremely concerning to our ranchers, and this outbreak could drive the price of food even higher. Unfortunately, we continue to see the fallout of the blunt and ill-considered cuts to federal workers, from the return of New World Screwworm to the United States, to farmers showing up to closed or understaffed Farm Service Agency offices, to attacks on our nuclear safety programs putting national security at risk. I will continue to hold the White House accountable, as I did this week during the U.S. House Appropriations Subcommittee on Financial Services and General Government hearing with Mr. Vought.

For 250 years, our great experiment has faltered, flourished, evolved, and progressed. The American experience is ever-changing and as diverse as the people who call this country home. But one thing has remained constant – the idea of America has always been a beacon of hope. Protecting this country and the ideals and values it was founded on takes work. Democracy is demanding. It takes dedication and principle. And it takes the resounding belief that upholding those ideals and values is worth the fight because America is bigger than any one person. Because liberty can only truly endure when it is paired with responsibility, virtue, and a commitment to put public good ahead of personal ambition. Today, we celebrate the moment when our founding fathers openly declared that creating this country, based in liberty, was a necessity in the face of tyranny. Their legacy is that leadership requires courage when it’s difficult, integrity when no one is watching, and a willingness to put country above self. We must remember that our duty is not merely to the next election, but to the next generation. That should be the challenge for all Americans as we look forward to another 250 years. From Massachusetts, where the fight for freedom first began, I wish you a happy 4th of July. God Bless America always, God Bless all who call her home, and God Bless our courageous men and women in uniform who continue the fight for liberty today.

On Monday, our office suffered an unimaginable loss. Chris Matthews, my District Outreach and Communications Director, passed away unexpectedly. If any one of you begin to lose faith in our country, remember Chris Matthews. Remember he was without question one of the Commonwealth’s sharpest political minds – a generational talent. Remember that he was more than a Congressional aide. He took the belief that through our actions we all can bring needed change and brought it with him on many interstate bus rides to canvas distant pivotal states and to the doors of the families he inspired. Remember through his example that public service is a genuinely noble vocation. As a trusted member of our office, he helped countless veterans, families, and those who could not advocate for themselves. Those of us privileged to have worked with him for over fifteen years will remember his laugh and his wry, often biting, humor – contrasting the way things are to the way they could be. We will always remember his authentic belief that in this country, people can bring about progress and meaningful change. It was real to him and his sincerity shown through. Chris was a genuinely good person. He was family to all of us, and we are devastated by his loss, particularly at such a young age. Our thoughts and prayers are with Molly and Eli and the many who loved him. Though we wish we had more time with him, his memory will continue to give us faith that one person can significantly make better the lives of those around him.

C001098.text: There’s confusion about how the cap and Associated Entity language work in the Protect College Sports Act. Let me clear it up. The cap is a hard cap. Full stop. That loophole is closed. Once a school hits the cap, a player can still do NIL deals on the open market — if the deal is genuinely commercial and the school isn’t directing it. That’s the line. Some commissioners want more: bar any company doing business with a school from signing that school’s players. So a QB couldn’t sign with Nike because Nike has a separate contract with his university. That’s not protecting a cap. That’s blocking a kid from selling his own name. Every pro league works this way. If the team doesn’t direct it, the player earns it. What exactly is the objection? And we went further than anyone asked: players disclose all of their deals, and the university president AND the sponsor sign a letter certifying they stayed under the cap. Cheat, and you signed your name to it. Hard cap. Loophole closed. Players keep the right to earn what the school didn’t arrange. Those aren’t in tension — that’s the whole point.

F000466.text: Affordability is about whether families can put down roots, businesses can grow, and communities can thrive. Our work with Maygan Best of New Hope began last September, when she turned a deeply personal battle with Crohn’s disease into a shared mission to improve care for patients and families. This week, we came together again with the Crohn’s & Colitis Foundation—not simply to continue the conversation, but to move solutions forward. We discussed the Safe Step Act, which I co-sponsor, to end dangerous step-therapy delays and ensure treatment decisions remain where they belong: between patients and their doctors, not insurance companies. We also focused on protecting medical research funding, because the next breakthrough treatment—or cure—depends on supporting science, not sidelining it. I am grateful for Maygan’s continued partnership and for the firsthand perspective she brings to this work. Together, along with the Crohn’s & Colitis Foundation, and advocates from across our community, we will keep fighting to ensure no patient’s care is delayed, denied, or placed beyond reach.

H001066.text: The fight for an affordable America starts by listening to the people living it every day. This law is a real step forward to build more homes, cut red tape, lower costs, and expand pathways to homeownership. Nevada’s housing crisis will not be solved overnight, but we are making progress, and I will keep fighting so working families can afford to live in the communities they help build. #NV04 https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-07-23/us-mortgage-rates-rise-extending-gains-for-third-straight-week?srnd=homepage-americas

The SAVE Act is not a voter ID bill. It’s a voter suppression bill that would force eligible Americans to prove their citizenship with documents millions of people do not have. Changed your name when you got married? Your ID probably doesn’t match your birth certificate. Now you have another bureaucratic mess to untangle before you can vote. Do not have a passport? Now you may have to spend money, track down old records, and jump through even more hoops to exercise your constitutional right to vote. You should not have to buy a passport to vote. You should not have to order a new birth certificate to vote. You should not have to prove your citizenship all over again when the government already knows you are a citizen. If you are eligible to vote, you should be able to vote. It’s that simple. The SAVE Act has one goal: make it harder for you to do that.

On this day in history in 1945, the USS Indianapolis is sunk by a Japanese submarine after carrying the atomic bomb across the Pacific Ocean. The cruiser was en route to the Philippines when one torpedo took the bow of the ship off followed by a second that hit the midsection and blew the ship nearly in two. The USS Indianapolis sunk in 12 minutes, with 300 of its almost 1,200 person crew going down with it. The remaining 890 fought to survive for four days before the Navy learned of the catastrophic event. During this time, the crew faced saltwater poisoning, dehydration, and shark attacks. By the time they were rescued, there were only 316 survivors, making it the greatest loss at sea from a single ship in the history of the US Navy, as well as the “worst shark attack in history.”

M001228.text: RT by @RepMaloyUtah: On Pioneer Day, I had the opportunity to tour Beaver and see firsthand the devastating impact of both wildfire and flooding. Standing in those burned and flooded landscapes, talking with the Forest Service personnel, local leaders, and the people of Beaver one thing was crystal clear: forest management works. The difference between treated and untreated forest was visible. Areas that had been thinned or otherwise managed gave firefighters a chance. They slowed the fire, reduced its intensity, helped crews establish containment lines, and in some cases, stopped the fire altogether. In the overgrown, untreated areas, the fire burned hotter, moved faster, and left behind far greater destruction, burning an unprecedented 70,000 acres in two days. It's frustrating that while the United States is the world's largest importer of lumber and paper products, millions of acres of our own forests sit overcrowded and vulnerable to catastrophic wildfire. The boots-on-the-ground Forest Service personnel managing these forests know what needs to be done and want to actively manage these lands, but too often commonsense projects are delayed or stopped by endless litigation and opposition by environmentalists and bureaucrats in Washington D.C. That's why the Fix Our Forests Act deserves to move forward. The legislation passed the House with strong bipartisan support, but has been stalled in the Senate for 18 months. It needs to move forward. I'm grateful to Congresswoman Celeste Maloy for bringing us together to see this firsthand, and to the Trump Administration officials who came to Utah to witness these conditions on the ground. With the U.S. Forest Service headquarters coming to Utah, we have a tremendous opportunity to ensure the people making decisions about our forests are closer to the landscapes and communities they serve. Thank you to USDA's Michael Boren, Sam Crofts from the Bureau of Land Management, and Chairman Bruce Westerman of the House Natural Resources Committee for taking the time to be there and hear directly from those who have been impacted by this catastrophe. On Pioneer Day weekend, that lesson feels especially meaningful. The pioneers who settled this state understood that stewardship requires hard work, planning, and taking responsibility for the land we call home. We honor their legacy not by leaving our forests untouched until they burn and cause catastrophic damage, but by actively caring for them so they remain healthy for generations to come. The Beaver community continues to show incredible resilience. I was reminded why I'm so proud to be a Utahn. We face challenges head-on, we help our neighbors, and we don't shy away from doing the difficult work that's necessary to protect our communities and our public lands. @realDonaldTrump @RepMaloyUtah @RepWesterman @SenJohnCurtis @RepBurgessOwens @RepMikeKennedy @USDA @forestservice @Interior @BLMNational @NatResources @JStuartAdams @cralbrecht52 @BeaverCountyUT

ROAD TO 250: Long Island & Queens Legacies Target Rock in Lloyd Harbor is more than a scenic landmark—it is a reminder of Long Island’s place in our nation’s history. The wildlife refuge takes its name from a 14-foot-tall glacial boulder standing just offshore in Huntington Bay. For generations, the rock served as a navigation marker for mariners and was reportedly used for cannon and target practice during both the Revolutionary War and the War of 1812. During the American Revolution, the British established "East Fort" nearby to help defend the harbor, and Lloyd Neck became home to Loyalists displaced by the conflict. As America approaches its 250th anniversary, places like Target Rock help tell the story of how the Revolutionary War shaped communities here on Long Island and across the nation.

B001323.text: This landmark investment by the U.S. Space Force is a tremendous win for Alaska and America’s national security! The Pacific Spaceport Complex-Alaska in Kodiak is uniquely positioned to support rapid, responsive launch capabilities. I’ve had the opportunity to personally tour our Kodiak spaceport and see firsthand the incredible potential of this facility. It's clear that Alaska offers a strategic advantage few places in the world can match, with the infrastructure and geography to support the next generation of defense and space innovation. As a member of the House Science, Space and Technology Committee, I am a continuous advocate for our spaceport. Today’s announcement serves as a reinforcing confirmation of Alaska’s indispensable role in America’s space economy.

This week, I had the opportunity to meet with @NASAAdmin Jared Isaacman to discuss the future of American leadership in space and the critical role Alaska will play in that mission.   As a member of the @housescience Committee, I'm committed to ensuring Alaska has a seat at the table as Congress works to support the future of America's space program.   Our nation is entering a new era of exploration in space, and Alaska is uniquely positioned to help lead the way. We discussed the tremendous potential of the Kodiak Spaceport Complex, one of the nation's critical commercial launch sites, as well as Poker Flat Research Range outside of Fairbanks, the world's only university-owned rocket range and a cornerstone of atmospheric and space research.   As investment in aerospace continues to grow, we have an incredible opportunity to prepare Alaska's students, engineers and technicians for high-paying careers right here at home. By strengthening partnerships with NASA, our universities, our military installations, and the private sector, we can ensure Alaska remains a key player in space innovation.   I appreciate Administrator Isaacman taking the time to discuss our shared vision and look forward to working together to ensure Alaska continues to serve as a vital launch point for discovery and as a key component in our nation's space leadership strategy.

Instead of betting everything on one proposal, they invite more innovators to compete and reward those who prove they can deliver. If we're going to compete and win, we need a research enterprise that is accountable, strategic, and focused on advancing American leadership.

I was honored to welcome my friend, the Ambassador of Hungary to the United States, @_SzabolcsTakacs to Haralson County today. In the late 1800s, dozens of Hungarian families moved from Pennsylvania's coal mines to Haralson County to establish a wine-making community.  They named their village Budapest after the Hungarian capital, and planted vineyards across the surrounding hillsides.  After Prohibition was enacted in the 1920s, many of the families left, and all that remains from that era is a home which once served as a Catholic rectory and the historic Budapest cemetery.  Today, we visited both. Ambassador Takács' visit is a special moment in Haralson County's rich history, and I am grateful for the incredible support the Haralson County Historical Society, the Hungarian Community Church of Georgia, the Dogwood Hills team, and local officials and community leaders provided to facilitate this meaningful event. Thank you, Ambassador Takács, for visiting Georgia's 3rd Congressional District, and thank you for strengthening the relationship between Hungary and the United States of America! @HungaryinUSA

This is a tremendous victory for Georgia's farmers, ranchers, and small meat processors. Yesterday, Georgia became one of only a handful of states participating in the Cooperative Interstate Shipment Program—allowing qualifying state-inspected meat processors to ship USDA-labeled products nationwide. For too long, a handful of massive processors have dominated the market, putting family-owned processors at a disadvantage. This is another step toward expanding opportunity, strengthening rural America, increasing competition, and rebuilding America's food production capacity. Under Biden, the United States flipped from net agricultural exporter to net importer. Four years of weakness turned a historic American strength into a strategic vulnerability. We’re fixing that. Food security is national security. Thank you Georgia!!! 🥩🐂🇺🇸

A phenomenal performance by Dilip Mahadu Gavit! Congratulations to him on winning the Gold Medal in the Men’s 100m T47 event with a remarkable timing, setting a new Games Record and achieving his Season Best. His speed, determination and dedication have made our nation proud. Best wishes for his future endeavours! #CWG2026

A superb Silver for Mohammed Basil Morssinganakath! What a sprint and display of determination! Congratulations to him for the success and also achieving his Season Best. His success reflects his hard work and focus. May he continue to scale new heights in the times to come. #CWG2026

WORLD_FRANCE_PRESIDENT.text: La France condamne avec la plus grande fermeté les frappes russes qui ont tué des civils en Ukraine, ainsi que la violation de l’espace aérien polonais. Notre soutien à l’Ukraine et à nos alliés ne faiblira pas, @ZelenskyyUa @donaldtusk. Il en va de notre sécurité collective.

Face à l’épreuve qui frappe le Japon, la France exprime sa profonde solidarité au peuple japonais. Nos pensées vont aux victimes, à leurs proches et à tous ceux qui sont mobilisés pour sauver des vies.
